extracted.intended_audience: NPR journalists and staff (reporters, editors, social media and visuals teams) who use social media for reporting or public-facing activity
extracted.subtask_description: Organizational guidelines for how NPR journalists should behave on social media and how to use social platforms as reporting tools, covering tone, accuracy, transparency, legal considerations, and safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence in social media practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media platforms are valuable parts of reporting and audience engagement but must be handled with the same diligence as other reporting tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use social media to speed research, extend contacts, and increase transparency. Do not cite anonymous social posts as finished reporting; you may use them to guide reporting but must carefully attribute what you cite and be clear about what NPR has and hasn't confirmed. When mentioning social media discussions on air, treat them as indicative of tone or reaction, not as a scientific survey or substitute for in-depth reporting. Understand and respect communities you enter on social media; act as a guest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respectful tone and language
rubrics_metrics.description: Words matter — strike the right tone online; be civil and professional as you would offline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid shouting (ALL CAPS), foul language, personal attacks, and baiting trolls. Pause and re-read before replying. There is modest room for looser language if tone and intent are appropriate (e.g., words like 'badass' can be acceptable in context), but always prioritize civility. When critical of colleagues, speak to them privately rather than airing criticism on social media. In internal platforms (e.g., Slack), ask whether you'd say the same to someone's face or in front of coworkers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not feed trolls / handling abusive behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: When encountering abusive or threatening communications, do not escalate or respond in kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a message is unpleasant but non-threatening, try a de-escalating response such as 'I appreciate constructive feedback. Can you tell me more about what concerned you?' If the user remains abusive, stop the conversation. If a message feels threatening, do not respond; forward it to the internal distribution list 'NPRThreats' for Legal, Security and News Operations review. Support is available to journalists under attack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect community norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Different online communities have distinct cultures and etiquette; be knowledgeable and adapt appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive to learn each platform's culture and be aware of gaps in your understanding. Consider how your behavior in a community will affect reporting; adjust language and demeanor as would be appropriate in comparable offline settings. Treat the community as a guest would treat a host and follow 'indigenous customs' of that community when reporting there.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and skepticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not simply spread information found on social media; verify, add context, and be transparent about confirmation status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When pointing to what others are saying, understand that many will view you as effectively reporting it. Tell readers what has and hasn't been confirmed (examples of phrasing provided). Challenge those posting information to provide evidence, raise doubts, and ask questions. Decide whether you are spreading a thinly-sourced rumor or passing credible (even if unverified) information with appropriate caveats. Act as if what you post is information you'd put on air or in an NPR.org story: provide context, attribution, clarification and corrections when needed. When in doubt, consult the Social Media Team.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about sourcing and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit about what was obtained from original reporting versus what was found on social platforms and explain how material was checked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell out how information was checked and why sources are considered credible. Invite audience assistance for monitoring and verification, but do not allow crowdsourced claims to determine reporting. When appropriate, follow up online leads with phone or in-person interviews to confirm identity, origin, and meaning. The Social Media Team can assist in verifying credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution with images and video from social media
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat images and videos posted online as potentially manipulated or misattributed; verify before publishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume online images/videos may be inauthentic. Verify when it was posted, whether it matches material distributed by professionals, whether it's original or a copy, and whether the poster has legal rights to distribute it. When in doubt, do not publish. Consult NPR's Visuals Team, Social Media Team, and Legal when appropriate. Reference NPPA code of ethics for additional guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty about identity and intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Be open about your employment with NPR when doing work related to NPR on social media; do not hide that you work for NPR or use pseudonyms for journalistic work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use pseudonyms when engaging online as part of NPR work. Journalists may use screen names in personal contexts, but they must identify themselves before using information gathered there in NPR reporting and must seek permission to quote. Remember that nothing online is truly private and personal behavior can reflect on NPR; avoid actions that could undermine credibility or impartiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-the-record expectations for online sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: When contacting sources online, prefer on-the-record interactions and be clear about the status of the exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat virtual interactions like real-world interviews: make on-the-record expectations clear to potential sources when reaching out. Apply the same standards of attribution and verification as with offline sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability for public social media activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything posted or associated with you online is potentially public and represents you and NPR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct yourself as if you might have to defend your online behavior publicly. Be mindful of friend/like choices, and how private posts can be circulated beyond intended audiences. When in doubt, consult your supervisor, the Standards & Practices editor, or the Social Media Team. Follow NPR's Guiding Principles in all social media activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality and political neutrality
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not advocate for political issues online or express personal political views you could not put on air or on NPR.org.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies even if you post under a pseudonym or personal account where your identity isn't obvious. Participation in groups may be seen as endorsement; consider observing rather than joining. If you follow or 'friend' partisan or advocacy accounts for beats, do so to monitor and follow comparable accounts on the other side as well. Be clear when joining that your purpose is information-gathering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal considerations and terms of service
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that social platforms' terms of service and legal rules affect what you post and what the organization can do with material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The platform's terms apply to content posted and gathered; they may allow material to be used in ways you did not intend. Law enforcement may obtain reporting via subpoena. Treat ephemeral-post platforms (e.g., Snapchat) as potentially persistent. Keep sensitive work material controlled and be vigilant about legal implications of online activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation risk when repeating or commenting on third-party content
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists can be legally responsible for statements they repeat; retweets may be protected under Section 230 in some views, but adding a defamatory remark can destroy that protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful when retweeting or reposting potentially defamatory material. Understand that merely retweeting may be seen as endorsing; use quote tweets to add context and clarify that you are pointing to another person's post. Avoid adding comments that could transform reposted content into your own defamatory statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quote tweets to provide context and avoid unintended endorsement
rubrics_metrics.description: A retweet can be perceived as an endorsement; use the quote-tweet function to add context and clarify NPR's stance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When retweeting, add explanation or caveats so audiences understand whether NPR vouches for the content. Don't assume a retweet will not be viewed as endorsement; be explicit when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult the Social Media Team when unsure
rubrics_metrics.description: When unclear how to apply journalistic principles in social media contexts, seek assistance from the designated Social Media Team.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Social Media Team has expertise in verifying voices and information from social platforms and can advise on credibility assessment and sourcing. Contact via SocialMediaTeam@npr.org. When in doubt about verification or platform-specific issues, consult them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect personal and professional privacy appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Use available privacy tools and safeguards but do not be complacent; assume content can become public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the highest level of privacy settings where appropriate to control access to personal activity, but do not rely on them to make risky statements. Consider how posts would look if cited in major outlets and avoid careless or libelous comments. Keep sensitive work materials secure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect copyrights and NPR content rules
rubrics_metrics.description: When posting about NPR work, link to NPR stories rather than copying full text or audio onto personal sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect NPR copyrights and terms of use: linking from a personal blog or profile to an NPR story is fine, but copying full NPR content to personal pages is not. Assume public-facing usage is subject to the same terms as general public users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral caution even in perceived private or anonymous contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume anonymity or privacy online; private communications can become public and reflect on you and NPR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid saying things online (or in emails) that you would not want publicly attributable to you. Public apologies may not undo reputational damage. Be circumspect even in seemingly private or anonymous exchanges.
